report.source_text: No evidence of lymphoma. Extensively necrotic fibrocollagenous tissue fragment showing mixed inflammation with predominance of neutrophils and eosinophils and collections of macrophages. Some evidence of vessel injury around the area of necrosis. Prominent necrotising lymphadenitis with karyorrhoectic debris and some palisading histiocytes, but no true granuloma formation. The surrounding mesenteric fat extensively infiltrated by lymphocytes, eosinophils and abundant histiocytes (but with no Langerhans cells). Early fibroblastic proliferation and evidence of damage to the mesenteric vessels noted.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A school-aged boy presented with a 2-day history of fever, central and lower abdominal pain, reduced appetite, and vomiting. Initial suspicion of appendicitis was excluded by ultrasound showing inflammatory changes between the stomach and pancreas. Laboratory investigations revealed anemia, lymphopenia, markedly elevated CRP (130 mg/L) and raised D-dimer (1126 ng/mL), with normal serum amylase and liver/kidney function. COVID-19 PCR was negative but serology was positive for SARS-CoV-2 IgG and IgM antibodies. Advanced imaging (echocardiogram, chest X-ray, abdominal CT) showed borderline low left ventricular function, mild mitral regurgitation, small pericardial effusion, globular heart, prominent perihilar vasculature, inflammatory mesenteric lymphadenopathy, mild splenomegaly, and inflammatory mesenteric fat changes. A biopsy of mesenteric tissue excluded lymphoma and showed necroinflammatory changes consistent with an inflammatory syndrome. The patient developed intestinal obstruction treated conservatively. Clinical context, exclusion of other diagnoses with biopsy, and evidence of systemic inflammation with cardiac involvement and positive COVID-19 antibodies supported PIMS-TS diagnosis. The diagnosis was further supported by clinical improvement following steroid treatment as noted in the longitudinal evaluation.
